report:
Conclusion: The claim is **plausible and moderately supported**, but mainly as “better bedroom ventilation improves sleep,” not as a universal rule that any open window/door helps. Small controlled and field studies link lower bedroom CO₂/better ventilation with improved objective sleep, perceived air freshness, less next-day sleepiness, and better concentration/logical performance (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26452168/). A 17-person field study specifically compared open window or internal door vs closed conditions and found ventilation-related differences in CO₂ and sleep measures (https://research.tue.nl/en/publications/windowdoor-opening-mediated-bedroom-ventilation-and-its-impact-on/). A later single-blind field intervention reported that increased ventilation in real bedrooms confirmed prior positive effects on sleep quality (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0048969723024269). However, a DTU review stresses the evidence base is still limited, with few bedroom-specific studies and inconsistent methods (https://orbit.dtu.dk/en/publications/reviewing-how-bedroom-ventilation-affects-iaq-and-sleep-quality).

Practical takeaway: opening a window/door may help if it reduces stuffiness/CO₂ and keeps the room cool, quiet, and clean. It may backfire with outdoor pollution, allergens, noise, cold drafts, security concerns, or fire-safety guidance favoring closed doors. Mechanical ventilation or airing the room before bed can achieve similar benefits.
